paper_style.palette_strategy: White background with black/gray structural marks; theory diagrams use restrained blue/green/red/violet semantics, result curves use green test, blue training, orange regularization, and violet total loss; tables remain monochrome and use rules/row labels rather than color.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Figure 1 and Figures 3–5 are vector PDF drawings; Figure 6 is composed of embedded raster panels on p.74; Figure 2 and Figure 7 are vector plot content. All object-bearing pages p.5, 9, 27, 33, 57, and 71–76 were rendered at 200 dpi.
paper_style.style_consistency: Main matter and appendix share ICML two-column typography, white backgrounds, and booktabs-like horizontal rules. Plot labels switch to DejaVu Sans-like glyphs in several objects; curve color semantics are consistent across Figures 2 and 7, while theory diagrams use local object-specific colors. Table precision and unlabelled ± dispersion are less consistent with self-contained captioning.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. An illustration of the learnability result in Theorem 2, applied to MPNNs by first mapping the space V1 (G) to a pseudometric space (via IDMs or computation trees; see Section K.1), satisfying Definition 1 and then applying Theorem 2. A computation-tree construction is shown on the right.

color.semantic_mapping: Black/gray marks structure and cover boundaries; blue, green, and red labels/points distinguish data, function/loss components, and selected nodes/edges.

encodings.facet: abstract space → learned function → computation tree
encodings.text: V₁(𝒢), Dataset(X), FΘ, f*, TIDM and error bounds

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual geometry rather than measured data: finite-cover points, a pseudometric neighborhood, a learned function class, and a computation-tree construction are shown; there is no sample aggregation or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduction finite-data/arbitrary-size motivation → Theorem 2 and Definition 1 → this cover-to-function-to-tree interface → Theorem 3/16 and Q1–Q3 result objects. The diagram supports the mechanism but does not prove that every MPNN satisfies the conditions.
design_strengths: The abstract space, training constraint, and computation-tree representation are arranged in a single left-to-right causal reading path.
Direct labels expose theorem symbols and avoid a separate legend.
design_weaknesses: All positions are schematic and uncalibrated, so cover geometry must not be read as quantitative data.
Small central loss arrows and color-coded node roles lose hierarchy in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Lay out abstract representation, learning constraint, and structured instance as a directed chain; print the theorem conditions beside the arrows and mark the geometry as schematic.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2. Training error and test score (lower is better) for size generalization experiments in Q1 using test datasets with 64 and 1024 nodes, respectively. Values were smoothed using Gaussian smoothing with σ = 1. The gray region indicates the loss values for which Theorem 4 guarantees extrapolation.

color.semantic_mapping: Green and blue are test scores at 64 and 1024 nodes; orange is training loss; gray fill and black dashed line mark the theorem-guarantee/minimum-loss region.

encodings.line: solid metric curves versus dashed theorem threshold
encodings.text: legend, axis labels, min. Training loss (2)

figures.data_and_statistics: Single-training-run Q1 trajectory with Gaussian smoothing σ=1: the plotted test scores are for 64- and 1024-node test sets and the orange curve is training loss. No seed spread, error bar, or uncertainty ribbon is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: §5 Q1 size-generalization question → Figure 2 optimization/test trajectories and theorem region → Appendix N Figure 7 and Table 6 full size slices. The figure is a headline interface but cannot replace the multi-seed table.
design_strengths: The log y-axis accommodates high initial loss, convergence, and low test scores in one panel.
The gray theorem region overlays a theoretical admissible range on the training trajectory.
design_weaknesses: Gaussian smoothing hides raw optimization fluctuation and no uncertainty band is provided.
64/1024 curves rely mainly on color, making grayscale discrimination weak.
figures.reusable_pattern: Overlay training metrics, cross-scale test metrics, and a theory-defined feasible region on one log-axis chart; state smoothing in the caption and put the complete scale grid in a table.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3. Bellman–Ford training graphs. Dots indicate omitted intermediate nodes, and edge weights are shown on the edges. (a) General path graph associated with w ∈ R^{K+1} as in Definition 13. The initial node is labeled a(v₀) = w₀, while all other nodes have label β ≫ 0. The path has length K with edge weights w₁, …, w_K. (b) Bellman–Ford training set for arbitrary K as defined in Definition 15, consisting of K + 1 path graphs corresponding to the scaled unit vectors xe₀^{K+1}, …, xe_K^{K+1}. Each path contains K + 1 vertices v₀, …, v_K. The root node satisfies a(v₀) = x if k = 0 and a(v₀) = 0 otherwise, while all other nodes have label β. Exactly one edge per path has weight x, and all remaining edges have weight 0.

color.semantic_mapping: Green nodes/β labels denote the path structure, red x marks the unique non-zero edge/root condition, gray marks zero/omitted structure, and black lines carry topology.

encodings.facet: general path versus K+1 basis-vector training family
encodings.text: w vectors, v labels, β, 0, x, and panel titles

figures.data_and_statistics: Constructive graph diagrams rather than measured data: panel (a) supplies one arbitrary path with w₀,…,w_K and panel (b) supplies K+1 scaled unit-vector paths. There is no aggregation statistic or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Theorem 16 K+1 constructive claim → Figure 3 path/basis-vector construction → Appendix E.4 theorem → Q1/Q3 training configuration and Figures 2/7. It is a method/reproduction interface, not a performance plot.
design_strengths: General and training paths use the same node and edge-weight vocabulary, making the sparse basis construction checkable.
The caption defines β, x, 0, omitted nodes, and the K+1 count.
design_weaknesses: The repeated K+1 family is abbreviated with ellipses, so the exact number cannot be enumerated from the drawing alone.
Color contributes to distinguishing x from zero and β; this weakens in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show one arbitrary instance and an isomorphic basis-vector training family, while defining node features, edge weights, and ellipsis semantics in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4. Edge case graph from Definition 30 for learning the K-fold Bellman–Ford update with higher aggregation dimension. The root node is v−1. Shown here is the instance for K = 4. At each node vi, i ∈ [K], the network can choose between multiple paths of equal total weight x.

color.semantic_mapping: Green main-path nodes, gray p-branch nodes, blue thick edges/x labels, and black zero-weight edges encode the equal-weight alternatives.

encodings.color: main versus branch and x versus zero edge role
encodings.text: node labels, edge weights, and K=4 title

figures.data_and_statistics: A single conceptual graph instantiates Definition 30 at K=4: one main path and multiple equal-total-weight alternatives. It contains no sample, aggregate statistic, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix F.2 one-dimensional aggregation limitation → Definition 30 → Figure 4 equal-weight alternatives → conjectural remedy/future-work boundary. The figure presents a failure mode, not an established empirical result.
design_strengths: The concrete K=4 instance makes the multiple-path ambiguity enumerable and visually traceable.
Thick blue weighted edges draw attention to the potential source of aggregation ambiguity.
design_weaknesses: Branch labels and zero weights are dense in one panel and there is no legend.
The caption does not repeat line/color semantics, so grayscale readers must inspect each edge label.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a small, enumerable edge-case network to expose a theoretical failure mode and state the instance parameter and epistemic status in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5. A compact space of computation trees enables algorithmic generalization. Under an appropriate metric on 𝒯, the computation trees Tsmall and Tlarge are close, so regularization-induced Lipschitz continuity of the model implies that good performance on the training instance Tsmall transfers to good performance on the nearby instance Tlarge. Occurrences of v in the computation tree other than the root are omitted for simplicity.

color.semantic_mapping: Black/gray lines encode graph and tree structure; pale blue/orange fills mark source/root nodes; violet and dotted gray neighborhoods encode proximity in compact tree space.

encodings.line: graph edges, tree branches, mapping arrows, dotted neighborhoods
encodings.facet: small graph/tree, large graph/tree, compact tree space
encodings.text: panel titles, Tsmall/Tlarge, 𝒯(compact), node labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual graph/tree/metric-space construction: small and large graphs are mapped to computation trees and then placed as nearby points in a compact space. No quantitative metric value, sample aggregation, or uncertainty is displayed.
figures.evidence_relation: Theorem 2/3 finite-cover and Lipschitz transfer → Figure 5 graph/tree/compact-space bridge → Appendix I MPNN classes → Figure 1 interface and Q1 experiments. It explains transfer but is not independent measurement.
design_strengths: Five panels move from graph to computation tree to metric space, making the abstract transfer argument scannable.
The thick arrows explicitly show the proposed small-to-large tree proximity relation.
design_weaknesses: The compact-space circles are schematic and have no metric values or threshold.
Purple/gray proximity hierarchy depends partly on color and becomes weaker in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Place the same object in raw graph, structured representation, and metric-space views; use arrows to show transfer and state which repeated nodes are omitted.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6. Weights associated with the two MPNN layers and the corresponding MLPs for Q1 with 1024 nodes in the test set. Bias values are not shown as they converge towards 0. 1st or 2nd denotes the MPNN layer, whereas layer 1 or 2 denotes the FNN layer.

color.semantic_mapping: Dark/light blue traces show learned weights and the zero baseline; black/gray axes and labels carry structure. Color is not used to assign named parameters.

encodings.text: panel titles and Weight Value/Training Steps axes

figures.data_and_statistics: Parameter-level traces from the Q1 1024-node test setting: eight panels cover update/aggr MLPs across the two MPNN layers, with biases omitted because they converge toward zero. The figure shows one trajectory set, not a seed aggregate or uncertainty estimate.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix N weight-matrix paragraph → Figure 6 parameter trajectories → Figure 7 loss dynamics and Table 4 hyperparameters. The traces expose a mechanism hypothesis but do not independently identify a causal regularizer effect.
design_strengths: All eight components use the same training-step direction, enabling layer-by-layer shape comparison.
The caption explains the omitted bias values and the two layer-index naming conventions.
design_weaknesses: Many overlapping lines lack parameter or seed identifiers, so individual weights are hard to track.
Different y ranges across panels complicate cross-component amplitude comparison, and the embedded raster can blur thin lines when scaled.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use fixed small multiples for module × layer parameter traces with a shared training axis; document omissions and naming in the caption without treating trajectories as causal evidence.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7. Extended results on size generalization obtained in Q1 for the General dataset. Each plot shows training error Lemp, training loss L, regularization loss ηLreg, and test score for each of the experiments. All plots are generated from the same seed and smoothed using Gaussian smoothing with σ = 1 (continued on next page).

color.semantic_mapping: Green/blue/orange/violet identify test score, training error, regularization error, and training loss; black dashed line marks minimum training loss/theorem reference.

encodings.y: test score/training and regularization errors/loss (log scale)
encodings.line: solid metric curves versus dashed reference
encodings.text: legend, panel captions, min. Training loss (2)

figures.data_and_statistics: Five General-dataset Q1 trajectories, with panels (a)–(c) on p.75 and (d)–(e) on p.76. Each panel uses one seed and Gaussian smoothing σ=1 for test score, training error, regularization error, and training loss; no seed uncertainty band is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 2 headline curves → Figure 7 complete General size decomposition → Table 6 exact test-score slices → §5 claim that test error does not increase with node count. The plot shows shape but one seed/smoothing cannot estimate cross-seed variability.
design_strengths: Consistent axes, colors, and four-item legends make five size panels directly comparable.
The caption states the same-seed and smoothing choices and flags the continuation page.
design_weaknesses: Four series rely strongly on color and there is no uncertainty ribbon.
The cross-page split interrupts reading and p.76 leaves large lower-page whitespace; reference text occupies a dense curve region.
figures.reusable_pattern: Expand every real test scale as same-axis small multiples, fix legend/color semantics, put aggregate numbers in a table, and disclose smoothing, seed, and continuation in the caption.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1. Test score results for Q2 with a standard and 1-iWL-equivalent MPNNs. All results were obtained across three seeds, and test scores are averaged. The number in brackets indicates the number of nodes for the test graphs.

tables.uncertainty: Three-seed mean with an unnamed ± dispersion; lower test score is better and no hypothesis test is shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: Q2 test scores for standard 1-WL and 1-iWL-equivalent MPNNs over ER-constdeg, ER, and General at 64/256/1024 nodes. Standard 1-WL is high (e.g. General 0.8393 to 0.8217), while 1-iWL is about 0.0030–0.0038.
tables.evidence_relation: Proposition 5 expressivity limitation → Q2 architecture contrast → Table 1 main values → Appendix Table 10 train/test decomposition. The table supports this pairwise contrast, not a ranking of all GNNs.
design_strengths: Dataset and node-size conditions are explicit in the column group and row labels.
The downward arrow and bracketed node counts reduce direction and scale ambiguity.
design_weaknesses: The ± statistic is not named.
Node-size grouping is conveyed by separator rules rather than a visible multi-level row header, requiring careful scanning.
tables.reusable_pattern: Put architecture in rows, datasets in a column group, and node size in row groups; state seed count, metric direction, and uncertainty definition in the table note.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2. Comparison of regularization between our ℓ1 based method (here named ℓreg ), ℓ1 and ℓ2 regularization terms. Across all experiments, η = 0.1 holds, and the MPNN from Q1 was used. Furthermore, the General dataset as outlined in Section N is used for all experiments. Results are obtained across three seeds.

tables.uncertainty: Three-seed mean with an unnamed ± dispersion; no significance test or interval is reported.
tables.data_and_statistics: General-dataset regularization comparison at η=0.1 using the Q1 MPNN and nodes 64–1024. ℓreg is about 0.0032–0.0033, ℓ1 about 0.0053–0.0061, and ℓ2 is larger and less stable (e.g. 0.0336 ± 0.0503 at 64 nodes).
tables.evidence_relation: Theorem 4 regularizer condition → Q3 loss replacement → Table 2 size-wise ablation → §5 discussion and Appendix Table 4/6 configuration slices.
design_strengths: Five node sizes make the generalization trend visible without a second table.
Short regularizer row labels keep the comparison compact.
design_weaknesses: The Reg. (↓) label and “regularization terms” wording require正文 context to relate the values to test score.
No best-row highlighting and no named ± statistic are provided.
tables.reusable_pattern: Fix dataset, architecture, and η in the ablation table, change one loss component, and report the component across the real size grid with an explicit uncertainty note.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3. Parameters for generation of Erdős–Reyni and stochastic block model (SBM) graphs in Q1 to Q3.

tables.uncertainty: Not applicable: generator parameters, not an estimator or repeated measurement.
tables.data_and_statistics: Graph generation protocol: n=64–1024; ER-constdeg p=6.4/n, ER p=0.1, star/complete have no p, SBM has the shown 3×3 probability matrix, and every graph uses Uniform(1,100) edge weights.
tables.evidence_relation: Q1–Q3 synthetic graph protocol → Table 3 generator choices → Figure 2/7 and Tables 1/2/6 test-set comparisons. It supplies distribution and denominator boundaries for replication.
design_strengths: ER, structured graphs, and SBM probabilities share one compact table and a common weight column.
The direct matrix cell preserves the SBM generator rather than reducing it to prose.
design_weaknesses: The SBM matrix is embedded in the p cell, mixing scalar and matrix visual levels.
The caption does not define dash/no-p semantics or node-set details.
tables.reusable_pattern: Summarize dataset×generator parameters in a compact row table, keep shared weights in one column, and define not-applicable symbols in the note.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4. Hyperparameter selection for each experiment in Q1 to Q3. Selected hyperparameters are highlighted, with the tuned ones shown in brackets.

tables.uncertainty: Not applicable: candidate and selected hyperparameters, with no measurement uncertainty.
tables.data_and_statistics: Learning-rate candidates {0.0001, 0.001, 0.01}; Adam; 160000 steps; batch 1; edge weight 50; initial node value 0; hidden dimensions {32,64,128}; 2 MPNN/MLP layers; first-layer output candidates {8,16,32}; second-layer output 1. Selected values are bold/bracketed.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix N training protocol → Table 4 candidate/selected distinction → fixed configurations underlying Q1/Q2/Q3 tables and Figures 2/6/7.
design_strengths: Q1/Q2/Q3 choices are aligned row-by-row and search spaces remain visible.
Bold selected values make the intended rerun configuration quickly scannable.
design_weaknesses: The note says tuned values are in brackets while braces also denote candidate sets, so the visual grammar is ambiguous.
The table spells the optimizer as “Optimzier.”
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep the search space and selected value side by side, but use one unambiguous highlight convention and define bold versus brackets explicitly.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5. Runtime and Memory Usage for each experiment in Section 5. The first value denotes the runtime in minutes (m) and seconds (s) of each experiment, and the second value denotes the used VRAM in MB. All results were obtained on a single computing node with an Nvidia L40 GPU and 120GB of RAM. For each experiment, the longest runtime was considered, obtained from test datasets with 1024 nodes.

tables.uncertainty: Not applicable: longest runtime and VRAM are reported, with no repeated-run uncertainty.
tables.data_and_statistics: Single-node resource surface: Nvidia L40 GPU and 120GB RAM; each cell is runtime m/s followed by VRAM MB, taking the longest runtime at 1024 nodes. Q1 General is 25m3s/891.55 and Q2 General 24m44s/887.95; unavailable Q3 ER-CONSTDEG/ER cells are -/-.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix N hardware paragraph → Table 5 cost surface → Q1/Q2/Q3 result objects. It informs reproducibility and resource budgeting, not scientific effect size.
design_strengths: Task×dataset alignment makes worst-scale resource comparisons direct.
The caption explains the order of the two values and the hardware boundary.
design_weaknesses: Slash-combined time/VRAM values are hard to parse automatically.
The note does not explain the reason for -/- cells.
tables.reusable_pattern: Bind runtime and VRAM in one task×dataset table and state hardware, worst-case selection, units, and missing-value semantics in the note.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6. Additional results for the ER-constdeg and ER dataset used for size generalization in Q1. Results are outlined for the given MPNN from Q1, with the test dataset changed accordingly. A list of hyperparameters can be found under Q1 in Table 4.

tables.uncertainty: Reported mean ± dispersion from the seed-based experiment; the table note does not name the dispersion statistic.
tables.data_and_statistics: Q1 MPNN with ER-constdeg, ER, and General test sets over 64–1024 nodes. ER-constdeg decreases 0.0035→0.0030, ER is about 0.0033–0.0038, and General stays about 0.0032–0.0033.
tables.evidence_relation: Figure 2 64/1024 examples → Table 6 full three-dataset/five-scale values → §5 Q1 size-generalization statement → Tables 3/4 protocol.
design_strengths: Dataset rows and node columns expose the size trend more completely than the headline plot.
The fixed Q1 model and Table 4 pointer make the comparison reproducible.
design_weaknesses: No best/change highlighting is used.
The ± statistic and seed aggregation are left to surrounding protocol text.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use dataset×scale matrices for full numerical slices and link them to the exact model/hyperparameter configuration used by the headline figure.

tables.label: Table 7

caption.text: Table 7. Additional results indicating test scores for the application of a three-layer MPNN as an extension of Q1 and the repeated application of a two-layer MPNN to learn four steps of Bellman-Ford. The MPNNs used are the same as in the experiments for Q1.

tables.uncertainty: Reported mean ± dispersion from the Q1 seed protocol; the statistic is not named in the caption.
tables.data_and_statistics: At General(64)/ER(64), three-step BF is 0.0075 ± 0.0023 / 0.0155 ± 0.0014, while repeated application is 0.0040 ± 0.0011 / 0.0051 ± 0.0013. It is a two-condition extension check, not a full depth sweep.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix N extension paragraph → Table 7 direct three-layer/repeated-application comparison → Table 9 two-layer three-step boundary and Figure 6 parameter mechanism.
design_strengths: The two extension strategies are directly paired under the same dataset/size columns.
The compact layout keeps the extra check from obscuring the main tables.
design_weaknesses: Only 64-node General/ER cases are shown, so the result cannot support a general K/depth claim.
The caption does not explicitly label the repeated-application row as the four-step case.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a minimal matched extension table with dataset(size) in the header and define the step semantics of every row in the caption.

tables.label: Table 8

caption.text: Table 8. Results indicating the application of the two-layer MPNN to real-world graph datasets Cora and Citeseer.

tables.uncertainty: Reported mean ± dispersion for the two-step BF score; the statistic is not named and no additional uncertainty breakdown is given.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two-step BF score is 0.0083 ± 0.0035 on Cora and 0.0080 ± 0.0040 on Citeseer. The row provides a real-world graph sanity check, not a new model comparison.
tables.evidence_relation: Appendix N real-world graph paragraph → Table 8 → Q1 synthetic-graph results. Cora/Citeseer should not be read as the General synthetic distribution.
design_strengths: Two real-world datasets are aligned in one direct comparison row.
The table stays visually simple and retains the common score precision.
design_weaknesses: The caption omits score direction, step protocol, and ± meaning.
No graph size or sample-count column defines the external-data coverage.
tables.reusable_pattern: Treat real-world datasets as a narrowly scoped matched row and state task, metric, and uncertainty semantics to avoid overgeneralizing a sanity check.

tables.label: Table 9

caption.text: Table 9. Results for the application of the 2-layer MPNN from Q1 to the prediction task of three Bellman–Ford steps. Following the same protocol as for Q1, the node features are given by the node values at the initial Bellman–Ford state. The target is given by the Bellman-Ford state after three steps.

tables.uncertainty: Reported mean ± dispersion from the Q1 seed protocol; the dispersion statistic is not named.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two-layer Q1 MPNN trained with the Q1 setup but evaluated against a three-step target on General: 1.5381 ± 0.0057 (64) decreases to 0.5721 ± 0.0039 (1024), remaining far above the two-step Q1 scores.
tables.evidence_relation: Q1 two-step setting → Appendix N three-step experiment → Table 9 failure boundary → Table 7 three-layer/repeated-application extensions. It links the numerical boundary to the one-layer-per-step theoretical discussion.
design_strengths: Five node sizes show that the error remains large even while decreasing with scale.
The note explicitly defines inherited node features and the three-step target.
design_weaknesses: A two-step Q1 reference row is absent, forcing cross-table comparison.
The ± quantity is not identified.
tables.reusable_pattern: Isolate an out-of-scope configuration in a size-wise failure table, define what stays fixed and what target changes, and include a reference row when space permits.

tables.label: Table 10

caption.text: Table 10. Additional results for Q2 with size generalization properties. The same setup as in Q1 was used in Q2, without special node labeling, unlike Q1.

tables.uncertainty: Reported mean ± dispersion for Q1/Q2 train/test rows; the statistic is not named and no significance test is shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: General size slices: Q2 training is fixed at 28.4869 ± 0.0015, Q2 test runs 0.8393→0.8217, Q1 training is 2.0544 ± 0.0151, and Q1 test is about 0.0032–0.0033. Q2 removes the special node label used in Q1.
tables.evidence_relation: Proposition 5/§3 expressivity → Table 1 Q2 test contrast → Table 10 train/test gap → §5 Q2 discussion. This table connects representation limitation to observed training/test behavior.
design_strengths: Q1/Q2 share node-size columns, and training/test rows make the gap visible.
The same General dataset and scale grid allow direct cross-row reading.
design_weaknesses: Training and test are encoded as separate rows rather than metric columns, so the comparison is less immediate.
The caption does not explain that training loss and test score are different quantities.
tables.reusable_pattern: For architecture contrasts, report train and test rows under shared dataset×scale columns and define metric units and label modifications in the caption.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 establishes the finite-cover/MPNN interface; Figure 2 gives Q1 headline dynamics; Tables 1 and 2 answer Q2/Q3 with matched expressivity and regularization comparisons; Figures 3–5 visualize constructive training, a higher-dimensional failure case, and computation-tree transfer; Tables 3–10 plus Figures 6–7 provide protocol, resources, parameter traces, full size slices, and extension boundaries. The strongest chain is general theorem → K+1 constructive Bellman–Ford set → matched empirical check.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions use italic Figure/Table labels followed by prose. Figure captions mostly explain setup and visual encoding; table captions mostly explain column conditions, seeds, hardware, or protocol. Figure 2/7 explicitly disclose Gaussian smoothing, but most result tables do not name the ± statistic and many captions require surrounding section context.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Result tables use two-level Dataset/Nodes headers or Nodes - General headers, with downward arrows in score columns and task/model/regularizer in row labels. Configuration tables use one-level headers. All tables use booktabs-like horizontal rules without vertical rules; Table 4 alone uses bold selected-value highlighting.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 3 visualizes Theorem 16 training paths; Figure 2/7 and Table 6 test Q1 size generalization; Table 1 and Table 10 test Q2 expressivity; Table 2 tests Q3 regularization; Table 9 and Table 7 separate depth/step failure from extension. Figure 6 exposes parameter trajectories but cannot substitute for matched ablation outcomes.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: The main text retains Figures 1–2, Tables 1–2, Q1–Q3, and the headline discussion. Appendix E/F/I Figures 3–5 carry formal construction and boundary mechanisms, while Appendix N Tables 3–10 and Figures 6–7 carry generator, hyperparameter, runtime, size, real-world, weight, and failure-extension details. Main-object interpretation therefore depends on Appendix N and the formal Definitions/Theorems.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Page typography and table typography are highly consistent; plot labels introduce DejaVu Sans-like text and Figure 6 is embedded raster, making thin weights more fragile than vector Figure 7. Caption/heading sizes remain broadly stable.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Figures 2 and 7 consistently map green to test score, blue to training error, orange to regularization error, and violet to training loss; theory diagrams use local green/red/blue/gray node and path semantics with positional/line-style support. Tables are monochrome. Grayscale reproduction is weakest for the four curve series.

most_reusable_patterns: Use a three-stage theorem → structured object → metric-space/transfer diagram, as in Figures 1 and 5, to connect formal conditions to later measurements.
Use consistent log-axis small multiples for training/test/regularization and a separate numerical size matrix, as in Figures 2/7 and Table 6.
Use matched row/column designs that change one architecture or loss component at a time, with Tables 3/4 defining the data-generation and hyperparameter denominators.
Use a general instance plus basis-vector construction for the minimal training set and isolate conjectural/failure boundaries in explicit objects such as Figure 4 and Table 9.
failure_patterns: Most result tables report mean ± an unnamed dispersion, making SD/SE/other spread impossible to identify from the object itself.
Figures 2 and 7 apply σ=1 Gaussian smoothing, and Figure 7 uses one seed with no uncertainty ribbon, so raw optimization/randomness is hidden.
Figures 4 and 5 use uncalibrated conceptual geometry; without caption/section context, schematic paths or compact neighborhoods could be mistaken for measured evidence.
Figure 6 has many unlabelled trajectories and embedded raster lines; Figure 7 is split across pages with large residual whitespace on p.76.
The linked public repository contains experiment/data/model code but no paper visual generation source or locked figure/table exporter, preventing object-level layout/color reproduction.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper uses restrained theory diagrams to establish finite-cover/MPNN mechanisms, unified log-axis curves and monochrome matched tables for Q1–Q3 evidence, and appendix objects for constructive sets, failure boundaries, resources, and full size slices.
